patterns.title: Inner and Outer Join Filtering
patterns.short_description: Combines rows from two or more tables based on related keys, using WHERE or ON predicates to isolate matched relational entities.
mental_triggers: Combine attributes from multiple related relational tables
Match primary key in one table with foreign key in another
Preserve all rows from left table while filtering right table matches (LEFT JOIN)
constraint_signals: Tables indexed on join keys allow nested loop or hash join in O(M + N)
Missing records should be filled with NULL (requires LEFT JOIN)
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M log N) or O(M + N) with index on join key | Space: O(M + N)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.department_name
FROM Employees a
LEFT JOIN Departments b ON a.department_id = b.id
WHERE b.is_active = 1;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def join_filter(employees: pd.DataFrame, departments: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = employees.merge(departments, left_on="department_id", right_on="id", how="left")
    return merged[merged["is_active"] == 1][["id", "name", "department_name"]]

patterns.title: Anti-Join (Exclusion Filtering)
patterns.short_description: Identifies rows in a primary table that have no corresponding match in a secondary table using LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, NOT EXISTS, or NOT IN.
mental_triggers: Find customers who never placed an order
Identify entities present in table A but missing in table B
Detect orphaned foreign keys or unused reference entries
constraint_signals: Nullable columns in secondary table can make NOT IN fail; NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL is safer and index-friendly
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M + N) with index-backed foreign key | Space: O(M) temporary set
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def anti_join(customers: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    active_ids = orders["customer_id"].dropna().unique()
    return customers[~customers["id"].isin(active_ids)][["name"]]

patterns.title: Grouped Aggregation
patterns.short_description: Partitions table rows by one or more dimension columns and computes summary statistics (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) per group.
mental_triggers: Calculate total sales per department or user
Find maximum transaction amount per day
Count distinct activities grouped by account status
constraint_signals: High-cardinality grouping requires memory hash table; pre-sorted input or index on GROUP BY keys avoids temporary files
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) or O(N) with index grouping | Space: O(K) where K is number of groups

patterns.title: Aggregate Filtering (HAVING)
patterns.short_description: Applies selection criteria to post-aggregation bucket metrics, filtering out aggregated groups that fail threshold conditions.
mental_triggers: Find classes with at least 5 students
Identify users whose total transaction sum exceeds $1,000
Select duplicate emails appearing more than once
constraint_signals: Filter conditions reference aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG) rather than raw individual row attributes
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for grouping + O(K) bucket filter | Space: O(K) groups
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT email
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def having_filter(person: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    counts = person.groupby("email").size().reset_index(name="cnt")
    return counts[counts["cnt"] > 1][["email"]]

patterns.title: Window Ranking Functions
patterns.short_description: Computes positional ordinal ranks across partitions without collapsing rows, distinguishing between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK().
mental_triggers: Find top 3 highest-earning employees in each department
Rank students by test score handling ties without skipping ranks (DENSE_RANK)
Assign sequential IDs to events per session
constraint_signals: Result requires retaining individual row identity while assigning rank values partitioned by department or category
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for window sorting | Space: O(N) window frame buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS 
FROM Scores;

patterns.title: Window Offset Access (LEAD and LAG)
patterns.short_description: Accesses values from preceding (LAG) or subsequent (LEAD) rows within an ordered partition without requiring self-joins.
mental_triggers: Compare current day temperature to previous day
Detect consecutive logons within 5 minutes of previous logon
Calculate day-over-day percentage change in revenue
constraint_signals: Chronological row comparisons where each row must inspect adjacent previous/next row within partition
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for ordered partitioning | Space: O(N) window frame buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
    SELECT num,
           LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS prev_num,
           LEAD(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_num
    FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = prev_num AND num = next_num;

patterns.title: Running Total and Moving Aggregates
patterns.short_description: Computes cumulative sums, moving averages, or bounded range sums over ordered rows using window frames (ROWS BETWEEN).
mental_triggers: Calculate cumulative bank balance across transaction history
Compute 7-day rolling average of daily user signups
Running total of items purchased over time per user
constraint_signals: ORDER BY inside OVER() creates cumulative frame (RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) by default
With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE, so tied rows share one running total; use ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for strict row-by-row totals.
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) for sorting | Space: O(N) window buffer

patterns.title: Top N Records per Group
patterns.short_description: Extracts the top or bottom N records within each category or partition using window ranking inside a CTE or derived table.
mental_triggers: Find top 3 highest paid employees in each department
Select most recent 2 orders for each customer
Identify top selling product in each category
constraint_signals: Requires subquery or CTE because window functions cannot appear directly in WHERE clause
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) window sort + O(N) outer predicate | Space: O(N) CTE materialization
patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, e.departmentId,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.departmentId ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Employee e
)
SELECT d.name AS Department, r.name AS Employee, r.salary AS Salary
FROM Ranked r
JOIN Department d ON r.departmentId = d.id
WHERE r.rnk <= 3;

patterns.title: Self-Join Relationships
patterns.short_description: Joins a table to itself to compare rows within the same dataset, such as manager-employee hierarchies or consecutive date entries.
mental_triggers: Find employees who earn more than their direct manager
Compare records with their own previous date entry without window functions
Graph or tree node relationships stored in a single table
constraint_signals: Single table contains both the entity and a foreign key pointing to another row in the same table
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) or O(N^2) unindexed | Space: O(N) intermediate join table
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.managerId = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

patterns.title: Gaps and Islands Detection
patterns.short_description: Groups consecutive sequential rows into contiguous islands or detects missing intervals (gaps) using ROW_NUMBER difference techniques.
mental_triggers: Find users with 3 or more consecutive days of active logins
Identify contiguous date ranges during which a machine was operational
Detect missing invoice numbers in a sequential sequence
constraint_signals: Subtracting ROW_NUMBER() from a date or sequence number yields a constant invariant for all rows in the same contiguous island
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N log N) window sort + O(N) group aggregation | Space: O(N) window tracking buffer
patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH Numbered AS (
    SELECT log_date,
           DATE_SUB(log_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY log_date) DAY) AS island_id
    FROM UserActivity
)
SELECT MIN(log_date) AS start_date, MAX(log_date) AS end_date, COUNT(*) AS streak_length
FROM Numbered
GROUP BY island_id;

patterns.title: Recursive Common Table Expressions
patterns.short_description: Iteratively evaluates anchor and recursive member queries to traverse graphs, hierarchies, or generate numerical sequences.
mental_triggers: Traverse multi-level organizational charts (CEO down to entry-level)
Generate a sequence of dates between start_date and end_date
Find all indirect connections or prerequisites in a graph
constraint_signals: Depth of tree or chain is arbitrary and not known at query authoring time; requires termination condition
patterns.complexity: Time: O(rows produced) | Space: O(rows produced) where the engine materializes the CTE

dialect_notes.mysql: cte_max_recursion_depth defaults to 1000, so long sequences such as date ranges need it raised or a different approach.

patterns.base_template_sql:
WITH RECURSIVE Hierarchy AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM Employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, h.depth + 1
    FROM Employees e
    JOIN Hierarchy h ON e.manager_id = h.id
)
SELECT * FROM Hierarchy ORDER BY depth, id;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def recursive_hierarchy(employees: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    roots = employees[employees["manager_id"].isna()].copy()
    roots["depth"] = 1
    levels = [roots]
    while True:
        curr = levels[-1]
        nxt = employees.merge(curr[["id", "depth"]], left_on="manager_id", right_on="id", suffixes=("", "_parent"))
        if nxt.empty: break
        nxt["depth"] = nxt["depth"] + 1
        levels.append(nxt[["id", "name", "manager_id", "depth"]])
    return pd.concat(levels, ignore_index=True)

patterns.title: Conditional Aggregation and Pivoting
patterns.short_description: Transforms row-level categorical data into column-level summaries using CASE WHEN expressions nested inside aggregate functions.
mental_triggers: Transpose row-based monthly sales into 12 distinct month columns
Count occurrences of different statuses in separate columns in a single row
Calculate proportion or ratio of specific events to total events
constraint_signals: Input is tall/narrow and target output is wide with fixed column headers for each category value
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) single-pass aggregate over groups | Space: O(K) where K is distinct groups
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT product_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store1" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store1,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store2" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store2,
       SUM(CASE WHEN store = "store3" THEN price ELSE NULL END) AS store3
FROM Products
GROUP BY product_id;

patterns.title: Date and Time Arithmetic
patterns.short_description: Performs interval manipulation, boundary extraction, and difference calculations across temporal fields using engine-specific date functions.
mental_triggers: Find records created within the last 30 days
Calculate duration in days or hours between order_date and ship_date
Group transactions by year-month or day of week
constraint_signals: Comparing dates must handle leap years, month boundaries, and timestamp vs date casting (e.g. DATEDIFF)
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) linear evaluation; can use index range scan if function is not wrapped on column | Space: O(1)

dialect_notes.general: Date and interval functions differ significantly across SQL engines (e.g. DATEDIFF in MySQL vs interval arithmetic in PostgreSQL).

patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT w1.id
FROM Weather w1
JOIN Weather w2 ON DATEDIFF(w1.recordDate, w2.recordDate) = 1
WHERE w1.temperature > w2.temperature;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def date_time_cmp(weather: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    weather["recordDate"] = pd.to_datetime(weather["recordDate"])
    weather = weather.sort_values("recordDate").reset_index(drop=True)
    date_diff = (weather["recordDate"] - weather["recordDate"].shift(1)).dt.days
    temp_diff = weather["temperature"] - weather["temperature"].shift(1)
    return weather[(date_diff == 1) & (temp_diff > 0)][["id"]]

patterns.title: String Manipulation and Pattern Matching
patterns.short_description: Performs pattern matching, case conversion, token concatenation, and regex validation on text columns.
mental_triggers: Find users with valid email format starting with a letter
Capitalize first character of names and lowercase remaining characters
Group comma-separated lists of products per user (GROUP_CONCAT)
constraint_signals: LIKE wildcards with leading % cannot use B-tree index; regex functions evaluate per row
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N * L) where L is string length | Space: O(L) output buffer

patterns.title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
patterns.short_description: Combines or compares row sets from multiple SELECT queries using set union, intersection, or difference semantics.
mental_triggers: Combine customers from active and archived regional databases
Find IDs that appear in both table A and table B (INTERSECT)
Find all items present in catalogue but never appearing in orders (EXCEPT)
constraint_signals: UNION removes duplicates with sorting/hashing; UNION ALL preserves all rows without duplicate removal overhead

patterns.title: NULL Values, COALESCE & Safe Comparison
patterns.short_description: Managing three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN) using COALESCE, IFNULL, IS NULL, and understanding aggregate NULL elimination.
mental_triggers: Customer Placing Largest Number of Orders: replacing NULL totals with 0 via COALESCE
Find Customers With Positive Revenue: filtering where column IS NOT NULL vs > 0
Aggregates ignoring NULL: COUNT(column) counts non-nulls whereas COUNT(*) counts rows
constraint_signals: Arithmetic with NULL produces NULL; comparing with = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(N) row evaluation | Space: O(1)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name, b.bonus
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Bonus b ON e.empId = b.empId
WHERE COALESCE(b.bonus, 0) < 1000;
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def null_handling(employee: pd.DataFrame, bonus: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = employee.merge(bonus, on="empId", how="left")
    merged["bonus"] = merged["bonus"].fillna(0)
    return merged[merged["bonus"] < 1000][["name", "bonus"]]

patterns.title: Correlated Subqueries & EXISTS Logic
patterns.short_description: Evaluating subqueries that reference columns from the outer query for each outer row, typically with EXISTS or scalar aggregations.
mental_triggers: Employees Earning More Than Their Department Average: correlated AVG in WHERE clause
Customers Who Bought All Products: NOT EXISTS (NOT EXISTS) relational division
Find Managers with At Least 5 Direct Reports: EXISTS / COUNT in subquery
constraint_signals: Correlated subqueries execute per candidate outer row unless rewritten by query optimizer into a join
patterns.complexity: Query Time: O(M * N) unindexed, O(M log N) with index | Space: O(1)
patterns.base_template_sql:
SELECT e.name
FROM Employee e
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Employee sub
    WHERE sub.managerId = e.id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
);
patterns.base_template_py:
import pandas as pd

def exists_subquery(employee: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    mgr_counts = employee["managerId"].value_counts()
    valid_ids = mgr_counts[mgr_counts >= 5].index
    return employee[employee["id"].isin(valid_ids)][["name"]]

patterns.title: Nth Highest Value via LIMIT/OFFSET & Functions
patterns.short_description: Extracting the Nth distinct record from an ordered dataset using DISTINCT with LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 or custom stored functions.
mental_triggers: Second Highest Salary: SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
Nth Highest Salary: encapsulated SQL function taking N and using OFFSET N-1
Returning NULL automatically if Nth highest value does not exist (wrapping in outer SELECT)
constraint_signals: Must use DISTINCT to ensure duplicate highest salaries do not consume multiple rank offsets
Wrapping query in subquery ensures returning NULL instead of an empty result set

patterns.title: DML Mutations (UPDATE, DELETE & Self-Referential Cleanup)
patterns.short_description: Modifying database tables in-place using DELETE with self-joins or UPDATE with conditional CASE expressions.
mental_triggers: Delete Duplicate Emails: DELETE p1 FROM Person p1, Person p2 WHERE p1.Email = p2.Email AND p1.Id > p2.Id

import pandas as pd

hints.title: Filter by Experience
hints.text: Filter candidate records who satisfy the minimum experience threshold before aggregating round scores.

hints.title: Join Rounds Table
hints.text: Join candidates with rounds on the shared interview identifier to pair scores with candidate profiles.

hints.title: Having Filter on Sum
hints.text: Group candidate identifiers and keep only those whose total score strictly exceeds fifteen.

hints.title: Complete Query
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT c.candidate_id
FROM Candidates c
JOIN Rounds r ON c.interview_id = r.interview_id
WHERE c.years_of_experience >= 2
GROUP BY c.candidate_id
HAVING SUM(r.score) > 15;
```

complexity.time: O(C + R) linear scan over candidates and interview rounds
complexity.space: O(U) storage for aggregated candidate scores
complexity.notes: Filters candidates by minimum experience and sums their round scores.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Aggregating rounds without filtering candidates first increases join cardinality.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Group aggregate with having clause minimizes intermediate record retention.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Candidate should recognize having filter for post-aggregation criteria.

solutions.code:

FROM Candidates c
JOIN Rounds r ON c.interview_id = r.interview_id
WHERE c.years_of_experience >= 2
GROUP BY c.candidate_id
HAVING SUM(r.score) > 15;
solutions.approach: Filter candidates by experience, join with interview rounds, group by candidate, and filter groups having total score strictly greater than 15.

FROM Candidates c
JOIN Rounds r ON c.interview_id = r.interview_id
WHERE c.years_of_experience >= 2

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def accepted_candidates(candidates: pd.DataFrame, rounds: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    cand_filtered = candidates[candidates['years_of_experience'] >= 2]
    merged = pd.merge(cand_filtered, rounds, on='interview_id')
    grouped = merged.groupby('candidate_id', as_index=False)['score'].sum()
    return grouped[grouped['score'] > 15][['candidate_id']]
solutions.approach: Filter candidate rows with experience >= 2, merge with rounds table, sum scores per candidate, and filter for total score > 15.

hints.title: Running Total Partitioning
hints.text: Calculate the running transaction sum partitioned by user account and ordered chronologically by day.

hints.title: Signed Transaction Amounts
hints.text: Treat deposits as positive amounts and withdrawals as negative amounts using conditional logic.

hints.title: Window Function Sum
hints.text: Use an aggregate window function over the partition to determine the balance after each transaction.

hints.title: Complete Query
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT
    account_id,
    day,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY day
    ) AS balance
FROM Transactions
ORDER BY account_id, day;
```

complexity.time: O(N log N) sorting transactions by account and day for window aggregate
complexity.space: O(N) window partition buffer and result set
complexity.notes: SUM window function computes running balance per account partitioned by account_id and ordered by day.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Correlated subqueries for running totals take quadratic O(N^2) time.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Window aggregation with partition and order achieves optimal linearithmic complexity.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Candidate should convert withdrawals to negative values inside SUM window function.

solutions.code:
SELECT
    account_id,
    day,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY day
    ) AS balance
FROM Transactions
ORDER BY account_id, day;
solutions.approach: Compute running balance per account using window SUM with conditional sign conversion.

solutions.code:
SELECT
    account_id,
    day,
    SUM(CASE WHEN type = 'Deposit' THEN amount ELSE -amount END) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY day
    ) AS balance

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def account_balance(transactions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = transactions.sort_values(by=['account_id', 'day']).copy()
    df['signed'] = df.apply(lambda r: r['amount'] if r['type'] == 'Deposit' else -r['amount'], axis=1)
    df['balance'] = df.groupby('account_id')['signed'].cumsum()
    return df[['account_id', 'day', 'balance']]
solutions.approach: Sort by account and day, compute signed amount, and calculate cumulative sum per account.

hints.title: Event Threshold Comparison
hints.text: A business is active if it records more than one event type whose frequency exceeds the overall average for that event.

hints.title: Event Average CTE with Having Count
hints.text: Compute the average occurrences per event type across all businesses. Join back and group by business identifier with having count > 1.

hints.title: Active Businesses Blueprint
hints.text: with AvgEvents as (select event_type, avg(occurences) as avg_occ from Events group by event_type) select e.business_id from Events e join AvgEvents a on e.event_type = a.event_type where e.occurences > a.avg_occ group by e.business_id having count(e.event_type) > 1.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH AvgEvents AS (
    SELECT event_type, AVG(occurences) AS avg_occ
    FROM Events
    GROUP BY event_type
)
SELECT e.business_id
FROM Events e
JOIN AvgEvents a ON e.event_type = a.event_type
WHERE e.occurences > a.avg_occ
GROUP BY e.business_id
HAVING COUNT(e.event_type) > 1;
```

complexity.notes: Grouped average per event type followed by hash equi-join runs in linear-logarithmic time.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Correlated scalar subqueries scanning the entire events table per row result in quadratic complexity.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Precomputing event type averages in a CTE enables direct inner join comparison.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Use of CTE or window AVG(occurences) OVER(PARTITION BY event_type) with HAVING COUNT > 1.

solutions.code:
WITH AvgEvents AS (
    SELECT event_type, AVG(occurences) AS avg_occ
    FROM Events
    GROUP BY event_type
)
SELECT e.business_id
FROM Events e
JOIN AvgEvents a ON e.event_type = a.event_type
WHERE e.occurences > a.avg_occ
GROUP BY e.business_id
HAVING COUNT(e.event_type) > 1;
solutions.approach: Event Mean CTE Join with Grouped Frequency Filter

WITH AvgEvents AS (
    SELECT event_type, AVG(occurences) AS avg_occ
    FROM Events
    GROUP BY event_type
)
SELECT e.business_id
FROM Events e
JOIN AvgEvents a ON e.event_type = a.event_type

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def active_businesses(events: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    avg_occ = events.groupby('event_type')['occurences'].transform('mean')
    above_avg = events[events['occurences'] > avg_occ]
    counts = above_avg.groupby('business_id')['event_type'].count().reset_index()
    res = counts[counts['event_type'] > 1]
    return res[['business_id']]
solutions.approach: Pandas Transform Mean and Filter with Count

hints.title: Distinct User Login Days
hints.text: A user may log in multiple times in a single day. Deduplicate to distinct (id, login_date) pairs first.

hints.title: Gaps and Islands Date Delta
hints.text: date_sub(login_date, interval dense_rank() over (partition by id order by login_date) day) yields a constant island date for consecutive sequences.

hints.title: Minimum Streak Threshold
hints.text: Group by id and the constant island date having count(*) >= 5 to filter active users.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH DistinctLogins AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date
    FROM Logins
),
RankedLogins AS (
    SELECT id, login_date,
           DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp
    FROM DistinctLogins
),
ActiveUserIDs AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM RankedLogins
    GROUP BY id, grp
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
)
SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.name
FROM Accounts a
JOIN ActiveUserIDs au ON a.id = au.id
ORDER BY a.id;
```

complexity.notes: Window ranking and date subtraction group contiguous days in linear-logarithmic time.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Five-way self-joins across consecutive dates scale poorly and fail to generalize cleanly.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: DENSE_RANK() date offset groups arbitrary streak lengths in a single pass.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Classic gaps-and-islands pattern subtracting rank offsets from dates.

solutions.code:
WITH DistinctLogins AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT id, login_date
    FROM Logins
),
RankedLogins AS (
    SELECT id, login_date,
           DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp
    FROM DistinctLogins
),
ActiveUserIDs AS (
    SELECT id
    FROM RankedLogins
    GROUP BY id, grp
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
)
SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.name
FROM Accounts a
JOIN ActiveUserIDs au ON a.id = au.id
ORDER BY a.id;
solutions.approach: DENSE_RANK Date Offset Gaps and Islands

import pandas as pd

def active_users(accounts: pd.DataFrame, logins: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    dl = logins[['id', 'login_date']].drop_duplicates()
    dl['login_date'] = pd.to_datetime(dl['login_date'])
    dl = dl.sort_values(by=['id', 'login_date']).reset_index(drop=True)
    dl['rn'] = dl.groupby('id').cumcount()
    dl['grp'] = dl['login_date'] - pd.to_timedelta(dl['rn'], unit='D')
    counts = dl.groupby(['id', 'grp']).size().reset_index(name='streak')
    active_ids = set(counts[counts['streak'] >= 5]['id'])
    res = accounts[accounts['id'].isin(active_ids)].drop_duplicates()
    return res[['id', 'name']].sort_values(by='id')

import pandas as pd

def find_pairs(relations: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m = pd.merge(relations, relations, on='follower_id', suffixes=('_1', '_2'))
    m = m[m['user_id_1'] < m['user_id_2']]
    if m.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame(columns=['user1_id', 'user2_id'])
    counts = m.groupby(['user_id_1', 'user_id_2']).size().reset_index(name='common')
    max_c = counts['common'].max()
    res = counts[counts['common'] == max_c][['user_id_1', 'user_id_2']]
    res.rename(columns={'user_id_1': 'user1_id', 'user_id_2': 'user2_id'}, inplace=True)
    return res

import pandas as pd

def average_selling_price(prices: pd.DataFrame, units_sold: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    merged = prices.merge(units_sold, on='product_id', how='left')
    valid = merged[(merged['purchase_date'].isnull()) | 
                   ((merged['purchase_date'] >= merged['start_date']) & (merged['purchase_date'] <= merged['end_date']))]

import pandas as pd

def bank_account_summary(users: pd.DataFrame, transactions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    spent = transactions.groupby('paid_by')['amount'].sum().reset_index().rename(columns={'paid_by': 'user_id', 'amount': 'out'})
    rcvd = transactions.groupby('paid_to')['amount'].sum().reset_index().rename(columns={'paid_to': 'user_id', 'amount': 'in'})
    df = users.merge(spent, on='user_id', how='left').merge(rcvd, on='user_id', how='left')
    df['out'] = df['out'].fillna(0)
    df['in'] = df['in'].fillna(0)
    df['credit'] = df['credit'] - df['out'] + df['in']
    df['credit_limit_breached'] = df['credit'].apply(lambda c: 'Yes' if c < 0 else 'No')
    return df[['user_id', 'user_name', 'credit', 'credit_limit_breached']]

import pandas as pd

def calculate_salaries(salaries: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    salaries['max_sal'] = salaries.groupby('company_id')['salary'].transform('max')
    def get_tax(max_s):
        if max_s < 1000: return 0.0
        if max_s <= 10000: return 0.24
        return 0.49
    salaries['tax'] = salaries['max_sal'].apply(get_tax)
    salaries['salary'] = (salaries['salary'] * (1 - salaries['tax'])).round()
    return salaries[['company_id', 'employee_id', 'employee_name', 'salary']]

import pandas as pd

def capital_gainloss(stocks: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    stocks['signed_price'] = stocks.apply(lambda r: -r['price'] if r['operation'] == 'Buy' else r['price'], axis=1)

    res.rename(columns={'signed_price': 'capital_gain_loss'}, inplace=True)
    return res

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def compute_rating(students: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    students['rank'] = students.groupby('department_id')['mark'].rank(method='min', ascending=False)
    students['count'] = students.groupby('department_id')['mark'].transform('count')
    denom = students['count'] - 1
    students['percentage'] = np.where(denom == 0, 0.0, np.round((students['rank'] - 1) * 100.0 / denom, 2))
    return students[['student_id', 'department_id', 'percentage']]

import pandas as pd

def confirmation_rate(signups: pd.DataFrame, confirmations: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m = pd.merge(signups, confirmations, on='user_id', how='left')
    m['is_confirmed'] = (m['action'] == 'confirmed').astype(float)
    res = m.groupby('user_id')['is_confirmed'].mean().round(2).reset_index()
    res.rename(columns={'is_confirmed': 'confirmation_rate'}, inplace=True)
    res['confirmation_rate'] = res['confirmation_rate'].fillna(0.0)
    return res

import pandas as pd

def consecutive_available_seats(cinema: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = cinema.sort_values(by='seat_id')
    free = df['free'] == 1
    prev_free = free.shift(1, fill_value=False)
    next_free = free.shift(-1, fill_value=False)
    res = df[free & (prev_free | next_free)]
    return res[['seat_id']]

import pandas as pd

def count_experiments(experiments: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    platforms = pd.DataFrame({'platform': ['Android', 'IOS', 'Web']})

import pandas as pd

def find_safe_countries(person: pd.DataFrame, country: pd.DataFrame, calls: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if calls.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame({'country': []})
    global_avg = calls['duration'].mean()
    c1 = calls[['caller_id', 'duration']].rename(columns={'caller_id': 'person_id'})
    c2 = calls[['callee_id', 'duration']].rename(columns={'callee_id': 'person_id'})
    all_calls = pd.concat([c1, c2], ignore_index=True)
    person['country_code'] = person['phone_number'].str.slice(0, 3)
    merged = all_calls.merge(person, left_on='person_id', right_on='id')
    merged = merged.merge(country, on='country_code')
    country_avg = merged.groupby('name_y')['duration'].mean().reset_index()
    res = country_avg[country_avg['duration'] > global_avg]
    return res[['name_y']].rename(columns={'name_y': 'country'})
solutions.approach: Pandas Concat and Double Merge Groupby

import pandas as pd

def customer_order_frequency(customers: pd.DataFrame, product: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = orders.merge(product, on='product_id').merge(customers, on='customer_id')
    df['spend'] = df['quantity'] * df['price']
    df['order_date'] = df['order_date'].astype(str)
    june = df[df['order_date'].str.startswith('2020-06')].groupby(['customer_id', 'name'])['spend'].sum().reset_index()
    june_qualified = june[june['spend'] >= 100]['customer_id']
    july = df[df['order_date'].str.startswith('2020-07')].groupby(['customer_id', 'name'])['spend'].sum().reset_index()
    july_qualified = july[july['spend'] >= 100]['customer_id']
    common = set(june_qualified).intersection(set(july_qualified))
    res = customers[customers['customer_id'].isin(common)][['customer_id', 'name']]
    return res

import pandas as pd

# Modify Person in place
def delete_duplicate_emails(person: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    person.sort_values(by='id', ascending=True, inplace=True)
    null_rows = person[person['email'].isna()]
    valid_rows = person[person['email'].notna()].drop_duplicates(subset=['email'], keep='first')

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

def employees_with_deductions(employees: pd.DataFrame, logs: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if logs.empty:
        return employees[['employee_id']]
    
    logs_copy = logs.copy()
    diff_sec = (pd.to_datetime(logs_copy['out_time']) - pd.to_datetime(logs_copy['in_time'])).dt.total_seconds()
    logs_copy['minutes'] = np.ceil(diff_sec / 60.0)
    
    worked = logs_copy.groupby('employee_id')['minutes'].sum().reset_index()
    merged = employees.merge(worked, on='employee_id', how='left')
    merged['minutes'] = merged['minutes'].fillna(0)
    
    res = merged[merged['minutes'] < merged['needed_hours'] * 60]
    return res[['employee_id']]

import pandas as pd

def eval_expression(variables: pd.DataFrame, expressions: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m1 = pd.merge(expressions, variables, left_on='left_operand', right_on='name', how='left')
    m2 = pd.merge(m1, variables, left_on='right_operand', right_on='name', how='left', suffixes=('_l', '_r'))
    def evaluate(row):
        op = row['operator']
        vl = row['value_l']
        vr = row['value_r']
        if op == '>' and vl > vr: return 'true'
        if op == '<' and vl < vr: return 'true'
        if op == '=' and vl == vr: return 'true'
        return 'false'
    m2['value'] = m2.apply(evaluate, axis=1)
    return m2[['left_operand', 'operator', 'right_operand', 'value']]
solutions.approach: Pandas Dual Merge and Rowwise Comparison

import pandas as pd

def exchange_seats(seat: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    n = len(seat)
    df = seat.copy()
    for i in range(0, n - 1, 2):
        temp = df.loc[i, 'student']
        df.loc[i, 'student'] = df.loc[i + 1, 'student']
        df.loc[i + 1, 'student'] = temp
    return df

import pandas as pd

def find_cutoff_score(schools: pd.DataFrame, exam: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m = pd.merge(schools, exam, how='cross')
    qual = m[m['student_count'] <= m['capacity']]
    if qual.empty:
        schools['score'] = -1
        return schools[['school_id', 'score']]
    grouped = qual.groupby('school_id')['score'].min().reset_index()
    res = pd.merge(schools[['school_id']], grouped, on='school_id', how='left')
    res['score'] = res['score'].fillna(-1).astype(int)
    return res
solutions.approach: Cross merge with capacity filtering in pandas

import pandas as pd

def find_interview_candidates(contests: pd.DataFrame, users: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    gold = contests["gold_medal"].value_counts()
    golds_3 = set(gold[gold >= 3].index)
    
    all_m = []
    for _, r in contests.iterrows():
        all_m.append((r["contest_id"], r["gold_medal"]))
        all_m.append((r["contest_id"], r["silver_medal"]))
        all_m.append((r["contest_id"], r["bronze_medal"]))
    df_m = pd.DataFrame(all_m, columns=["contest_id", "user_id"]).sort_values(["user_id", "contest_id"])
    
    streak_users = set()
    for uid, grp in df_m.groupby("user_id"):
        cids = sorted(grp["contest_id"].unique())
        streak = 1
        for i in range(1, len(cids)):
            if cids[i] == cids[i - 1] + 1:
                streak += 1
                if streak >= 3:
                    streak_users.add(uid)
            else:
                streak = 1
    candidates = list(golds_3.union(streak_users))
    res = users[users["user_id"].isin(candidates)][["name", "mail"]]
    return res
solutions.approach: Streak counting and set union in pandas

import pandas as pd

def median_frequency(numbers: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = numbers.sort_values(by='num')
    total = df['frequency'].sum()
    df['cum_asc'] = df['frequency'].cumsum()
    df['cum_desc'] = df['frequency'].iloc[::-1].cumsum().iloc[::-1]
    medians = df[(df['cum_asc'] >= total / 2.0) & (df['cum_desc'] >= total / 2.0)]
    med_val = round(medians['num'].mean(), 1)
    return pd.DataFrame({'median': [med_val]})

import pandas as pd

def same_day_calls(calls: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    c1 = calls.rename(columns={'caller_id': 'user_id', 'recipient_id': 'other_id'})
    c2 = calls.rename(columns={'recipient_id': 'user_id', 'caller_id': 'other_id'})
    all_calls = pd.concat([c1, c2])
    all_calls['date'] = pd.to_datetime(all_calls['call_time']).dt.date
    all_calls = all_calls.sort_values('call_time')
    
    first = all_calls.groupby(['user_id', 'date']).first().reset_index()
    last = all_calls.groupby(['user_id', 'date']).last().reset_index()
    
    m = pd.merge(first, last, on=['user_id', 'date'])
    same = m[m['other_id_x'] == m['other_id_y']]
    return same[['user_id']].drop_duplicates()

import pandas as pd

def gameplay_analysis(activity: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    first_logins = activity.groupby('player_id')['event_date'].min().reset_index()
    first_logins['next_date'] = first_logins['event_date'] + pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    merged = pd.merge(first_logins, activity, left_on=['player_id', 'next_date'], right_on=['player_id', 'event_date'])
    total_players = activity['player_id'].nunique()
    retained_players = merged['player_id'].nunique()
    fraction = round(retained_players / total_players, 2) if total_players > 0 else 0.0
    return pd.DataFrame({'fraction': [fraction]})

import pandas as pd

def gameplay_analysis(activity: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    installs = activity.groupby('player_id')['event_date'].min().reset_index()
    installs.rename(columns={'event_date': 'install_dt'}, inplace=True)
    activity['next_day'] = activity['event_date'] - pd.Timedelta(days=1)
    merged = installs.merge(activity, left_on=['player_id', 'install_dt'], right_on=['player_id', 'next_day'], how='left')
    res = merged.groupby('install_dt').agg(
        installs=('player_id', 'nunique'),
        retained=('event_date', 'count')
    ).reset_index()
    res['Day1_retention'] = (res['retained'] / res['installs']).round(2)
    return res[['install_dt', 'installs', 'Day1_retention']]
solutions.approach: Pandas Groupby Minimum and Offset Merge

import pandas as pd

def second_most_recent_activity(user_activity: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    user_activity = user_activity.sort_values(by=['username', 'endDate'], ascending=[True, False])
    user_activity['rn'] = user_activity.groupby('username').cumcount() + 1

import pandas as pd

def hopper_company_queries_i(drivers: pd.DataFrame, rides: pd.DataFrame, accepted_rides: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    months_df = pd.DataFrame({'month': list(range(1, 13))})
    drivers['join_date'] = pd.to_datetime(drivers['join_date'])
    rides['requested_at'] = pd.to_datetime(rides['requested_at'])
    merged_rides = rides.merge(accepted_rides, on='ride_id')
    rides_2020 = merged_rides[merged_rides['requested_at'].dt.year == 2020].copy()
    rides_2020['month'] = rides_2020['requested_at'].dt.month
    rides_count = rides_2020.groupby('month').size().to_dict()
    active_list = []
    rides_list = []
    for m in range(1, 13):
        end_of_month = pd.Period(f'2020-{m:02d}', 'M').end_time.date()
        act = len(drivers[drivers['join_date'].dt.date <= end_of_month])
        active_list.append(act)
        rides_list.append(rides_count.get(m, 0))
    months_df['active_drivers'] = active_list
    months_df['accepted_rides'] = rides_list
    return months_df

WITH RECURSIVE Months AS (

import pandas as pd

def hopper_company_queries_iii(drivers: pd.DataFrame, rides: pd.DataFrame, accepted_rides: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    months_df = pd.DataFrame({'month': list(range(1, 13))})
    rides['requested_at'] = pd.to_datetime(rides['requested_at'])
    merged = rides.merge(accepted_rides, on='ride_id')
    rides_2020 = merged[merged['requested_at'].dt.year == 2020].copy()
    rides_2020['month'] = rides_2020['requested_at'].dt.month
    monthly = rides_2020.groupby('month')[['ride_distance', 'ride_duration']].sum().reset_index()
    full = months_df.merge(monthly, on='month', how='left').fillna(0)
    full['average_ride_distance'] = (
        (full['ride_distance'] + full['ride_distance'].shift(-1) + full['ride_distance'].shift(-2)) / 3.0
    ).round(2)
    full['average_ride_duration'] = (
        (full['ride_duration'] + full['ride_duration'].shift(-1) + full['ride_duration'].shift(-2)) / 3.0
    ).round(2)
    res = full[full['month'] <= 10][['month', 'average_ride_distance', 'average_ride_duration']]
    return res

import pandas as pd

def immediate_food_delivery(delivery: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    idx = delivery.groupby('customer_id')['order_date'].idxmin()
    first_orders = delivery.loc[idx]
    immediate = (first_orders['order_date'] == first_orders['customer_pref_delivery_date']).sum()
    pct = round(100.0 * immediate / len(first_orders), 2)
    return pd.DataFrame({'immediate_percentage': [pct]})

import pandas as pd

def league_statistics(teams: pd.DataFrame, matches: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    home = matches[["home_team_id", "home_team_goals", "away_team_goals"]].copy()
    home.columns = ["team_id", "goals_for", "goals_against"]
    home["points"] = home.apply(lambda r: 3 if r["goals_for"] > r["goals_against"] else (1 if r["goals_for"] == r["goals_against"] else 0), axis=1)
    
    away = matches[["away_team_id", "away_team_goals", "home_team_goals"]].copy()
    away.columns = ["team_id", "goals_for", "goals_against"]
    away["points"] = away.apply(lambda r: 3 if r["goals_for"] > r["goals_against"] else (1 if r["goals_for"] == r["goals_against"] else 0), axis=1)
    
    all_m = pd.concat([home, away])
    agg = all_m.groupby("team_id").agg(
        matches_played=("points", "count"),
        points=("points", "sum"),
        goal_for=("goals_for", "sum"),
        goal_against=("goals_against", "sum")
    ).reset_index()
    agg["goal_diff"] = agg["goal_for"] - agg["goal_against"]
    
    res = teams.merge(agg, on="team_id")
    res = res.sort_values(by=["points", "goal_diff", "team_name"], ascending=[False, False, True])
    return res[["team_name", "matches_played", "points", "goal_for", "goal_against", "goal_diff"]]

import pandas as pd

def longest_winning_streak(matches: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if matches.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame({'player_id': [], 'longest_streak': []})
    matches = matches.sort_values(['player_id', 'match_day']).copy()
    matches['overall_rn'] = matches.groupby('player_id').cumcount() + 1
    wins = matches[matches['result'] == 'Win'].copy()
    if wins.empty:
        res = pd.DataFrame({'player_id': matches['player_id'].unique()})
        res['longest_streak'] = 0
        return res
    wins['win_rn'] = wins.groupby('player_id').cumcount() + 1
    wins['grp'] = wins['overall_rn'] - wins['win_rn']
    streaks = wins.groupby(['player_id', 'grp']).size().reset_index(name='streak')
    max_streaks = streaks.groupby('player_id')['streak'].max().reset_index(name='longest_streak')
    all_players = pd.DataFrame({'player_id': matches['player_id'].unique()})
    res = all_players.merge(max_streaks, on='player_id', how='left')
    res['longest_streak'] = res['longest_streak'].fillna(0).astype(int)
    return res

import pandas as pd

def market_analysis(users: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame, items: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    orders_2019 = orders[(orders['order_date'] >= '2019-01-01') & (orders['order_date'] <= '2019-12-31')]
    counts = orders_2019.groupby('buyer_id')['order_id'].count().reset_index()
    counts = counts.rename(columns={'order_id': 'orders_in_2019'})
    merged = users.merge(counts, left_on='user_id', right_on='buyer_id', how='left')
    merged['orders_in_2019'] = merged['orders_in_2019'].fillna(0).astype(int)
    merged = merged.rename(columns={'user_id': 'buyer_id'})
    return merged[['buyer_id', 'join_date', 'orders_in_2019']]

import pandas as pd

def market_analysis(users: pd.DataFrame, orders: pd.DataFrame, items: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    orders_sorted = orders.sort_values(by=['seller_id', 'order_date'])
    orders_sorted['rn'] = orders_sorted.groupby('seller_id').cumcount() + 1
    second_orders = orders_sorted[orders_sorted['rn'] == 2]
    second_items = second_orders.merge(items, on='item_id', how='left')
    merged = users.merge(second_items, left_on='user_id', right_on='seller_id', how='left')
    merged['2nd_item_fav_brand'] = merged.apply(
        lambda r: 'yes' if r['favorite_brand'] == r['item_brand'] else 'no', axis=1
    )
    merged.rename(columns={'user_id': 'seller_id'}, inplace=True)
    return merged[['seller_id', '2nd_item_fav_brand']]

import pandas as pd

def median_employee_salary(employee: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = employee.sort_values(by=['company', 'salary', 'id'])
    df['rn'] = df.groupby('company').cumcount() + 1
    df['cnt'] = df.groupby('company')['id'].transform('count')
    median_df = df[(df['rn'] >= df['cnt'] / 2.0) & (df['rn'] <= df['cnt'] / 2.0 + 1)]
    return median_df[['id', 'company', 'salary']]

import pandas as pd

def monthly_transactions(transactions: pd.DataFrame, chargebacks: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    app = transactions[transactions['state'] == 'approved'].copy()
    app['month'] = app['trans_date'].astype(str).str.slice(0, 7)
    app['type'] = 'approved'
    app_stream = app[['month', 'country', 'amount', 'type']]

    cb = chargebacks.merge(transactions, left_on='trans_id', right_on='id')
    cb['month'] = cb['trans_date_x'].astype(str).str.slice(0, 7)
    cb['type'] = 'chargeback'
    cb_stream = cb[['month', 'country', 'amount', 'type']]

    unified = pd.concat([app_stream, cb_stream])
    res = unified.groupby(['month', 'country']).agg(
        approved_count=('type', lambda x: (x == 'approved').sum()),
        approved_amount=('amount', lambda x: x[unified.loc[x.index, 'type'] == 'approved'].sum()),
        chargeback_count=('type', lambda x: (x == 'chargeback').sum()),
        chargeback_amount=('amount', lambda x: x[unified.loc[x.index, 'type'] == 'chargeback'].sum())
    ).reset_index()
    return res

    u_counts = movie_rating.groupby('user_id').size().reset_index(name='cnt')
    u_merged = u_counts.merge(users, on='user_id')
    u_sorted = u_merged.sort_values(by=['cnt', 'name'], ascending=[False, True])
    top_user = u_sorted.iloc[0]['name']

    # 2. Top movie in Feb 2020
    feb = movie_rating[movie_rating['created_at'].astype(str).str.startswith('2020-02')]
    m_avg = feb.groupby('movie_id')['rating'].mean().reset_index()
    m_merged = m_avg.merge(movies, on='movie_id')
    m_sorted = m_merged.sort_values(by=['rating', 'title'], ascending=[False, True])
    top_movie = m_sorted.iloc[0]['title']

    return pd.DataFrame({'results': [top_user, top_movie]})

import pandas as pd

def recommend_page(friendship: pd.DataFrame, likes: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    f1 = friendship.rename(columns={"user1_id": "user_id", "user2_id": "friend_id"})
    f2 = friendship.rename(columns={"user2_id": "user_id", "user1_id": "friend_id"})

def page_recommendations(friendship: pd.DataFrame, likes: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:

def price_at_given_date(products: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:

import pandas as pd

def queries_quality_and_percentage(queries: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    valid = queries[queries['query_name'].notnull()].copy()
    valid['ratio'] = valid['rating'] / valid['position'] + 1e-12
    valid['poor'] = (valid['rating'] < 3).astype(int) * 100.0
    res = valid.groupby('query_name').agg(
        quality=('ratio', lambda x: round(x.mean(), 2)),

    ).reset_index()

import pandas as pd

def report_contiguous_dates(failed: pd.DataFrame, succeeded: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    f = failed[(failed['fail_date'] >= '2019-01-01') & (failed['fail_date'] <= '2019-12-31')].rename(columns={'fail_date': 'date'})
    f['state'] = 'failed'
    s = succeeded[(succeeded['success_date'] >= '2019-01-01') & (succeeded['success_date'] <= '2019-12-31')].rename(columns={'success_date': 'date'})
    s['state'] = 'succeeded'
    df = pd.concat([f, s]).sort_values(by='date').reset_index(drop=True)
    df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
    df['grp'] = (df['state'] != df['state'].shift(1)).cumsum()
    res = df.groupby(['grp', 'state']).agg(
        start_date=('date', 'min'),
        end_date=('date', 'max')
    ).reset_index()
    res['start_date'] = res['start_date'].dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    res['end_date'] = res['end_date'].dt.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    res.rename(columns={'state': 'period_state'}, inplace=True)
    return res.sort_values(by='start_date')[['period_state', 'start_date', 'end_date']]

import pandas as pd

def team_scores(teams: pd.DataFrame, matches: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    p1 = []
    p2 = []
    for _, row in matches.iterrows():
        if row['host_goals'] > row['guest_goals']:
            p1.append({'team_id': row['host_team'], 'points': 3})
            p2.append({'team_id': row['guest_team'], 'points': 0})
        elif row['host_goals'] == row['guest_goals']:
            p1.append({'team_id': row['host_team'], 'points': 1})
            p2.append({'team_id': row['guest_team'], 'points': 1})
        else:
            p1.append({'team_id': row['host_team'], 'points': 0})
            p2.append({'team_id': row['guest_team'], 'points': 3})
    all_points = pd.DataFrame(p1 + p2)
    scores = all_points.groupby('team_id')['points'].sum().reset_index() if not all_points.empty else pd.DataFrame(columns=['team_id', 'points'])
    merged = teams.merge(scores, on='team_id', how='left')
    merged['num_points'] = merged['points'].fillna(0).astype(int)
    return merged.sort_values(by=['num_points', 'team_id'], ascending=[False, True])[['team_id', 'team_name', 'num_points']]

import pandas as pd

def airport_with_most_traffic(flights: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    dep = flights[['departure_airport', 'flights_count']].rename(columns={'departure_airport': 'airport_id'})
    arr = flights[['arrival_airport', 'flights_count']].rename(columns={'arrival_airport': 'airport_id'})
    comb = pd.concat([dep, arr], ignore_index=True)
    grouped = comb.groupby('airport_id', as_index=False)['flights_count'].sum()
    max_traffic = grouped['flights_count'].max()
    res = grouped[grouped['flights_count'] == max_traffic][['airport_id']]
    return res

hints.text: Buses arrive in order of arrival time, and passengers board in chronological order up to bus capacity.

hints.title: Compute Cumulative Waiting Counts
hints.text: Rank the buses by arrival time and compute the count of arriving passengers who arrived before or at each bus arrival time.

hints.text: Simulate boarding using a recursive common table expression where each bus boards up to its capacity from remaining waiting passengers.

hints.title: Complete SQL Query
hints.text:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE BusRank AS (
    SELECT 
        bus_id,
        arrival_time,
        capacity,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY arrival_time) AS rn
    FROM Buses
),
BusPassengers AS (
    SELECT 
        b.rn,
        b.bus_id,
        b.capacity,
        COUNT(p.passenger_id) AS total_arrived
    FROM BusRank b
    LEFT JOIN Passengers p ON p.arrival_time <= b.arrival_time
    GROUP BY b.rn, b.bus_id, b.capacity
),
BusNew AS (
    SELECT 
        rn,
        bus_id,
        capacity,
        total_arrived - COALESCE(LAG(total_arrived) OVER (ORDER BY rn), 0) AS new_passengers
    FROM BusPassengers
),
Sim AS (
    SELECT 
        rn,
        bus_id,
        CASE WHEN new_passengers < capacity THEN new_passengers ELSE capacity END AS boarded,
        CASE WHEN new_passengers > capacity THEN new_passengers - capacity ELSE 0 END AS waiting
    FROM BusNew
    WHERE rn = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 
        b.rn,
        b.bus_id,
        CASE WHEN (s.waiting + b.new_passengers) < b.capacity THEN (s.waiting + b.new_passengers) ELSE b.capacity END AS boarded,
        CASE WHEN (s.waiting + b.new_passengers) > b.capacity THEN (s.waiting + b.new_passengers) - b.capacity ELSE 0 END AS waiting
    FROM Sim s
    JOIN BusNew b ON b.rn = s.rn + 1
)
SELECT bus_id, boarded AS passengers_cnt
FROM Sim
ORDER BY bus_id ASC;
```

import pandas as pd

def count_passengers_in_bus(buses: pd.DataFrame, passengers: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    if buses.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame({'bus_id': [], 'passengers_cnt': []})
    b_sorted = buses.sort_values('arrival_time').reset_index(drop=True)
    p_sorted = passengers.sort_values('arrival_time')['arrival_time'].tolist()
    boarded_counts = []
    p_idx = 0
    n_p = len(p_sorted)
    for _, bus in b_sorted.iterrows():
        cap = bus['capacity']
        arr = bus['arrival_time']
        eligible = 0
        temp_idx = p_idx
        while temp_idx < n_p and p_sorted[temp_idx] <= arr:
            eligible += 1
            temp_idx += 1
        boarded = min(cap, eligible)
        boarded_counts.append(boarded)
        p_idx += boarded
    b_sorted['passengers_cnt'] = boarded_counts
    return b_sorted[['bus_id', 'passengers_cnt']].sort_values('bus_id')

solutions.code:
import pandas as pd

def number_of_seniors_and_juniors_to_join_the_company_ii(candidates: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    seniors = candidates[candidates['experience'] == 'Senior'].sort_values(by=['salary', 'employee_id'])
    seniors['running'] = seniors['salary'].cumsum()
    accepted_seniors = seniors[seniors['running'] <= 70000]
    spent = accepted_seniors['running'].max() if not accepted_seniors.empty else 0
    
    juniors = candidates[candidates['experience'] == 'Junior'].sort_values(by=['salary', 'employee_id'])
    juniors['running'] = juniors['salary'].cumsum()
    accepted_juniors = juniors[juniors['running'] <= (70000 - spent)]
    
    return pd.concat([accepted_seniors[['employee_id']], accepted_juniors[['employee_id']]], ignore_index=True)
solutions.approach: Pandas candidate filtering by cumulative budget

hints.title: Static Calendar Year Series
hints.text: Sales spans cover years 2018, 2019, and 2020. Construct or join against these three calendar years.

hints.title: Date Overlap Computation
hints.text: The active sales duration in year Y is datediff(least(period_end, concat(Y, "-12-31")), greatest(period_start, concat(Y, "-01-01"))) + 1.

hints.title: Revenue Aggregation by Year
hints.text: Multiply overlapping days by average_daily_revenue where period_start <= concat(Y, "-12-31") and period_end >= concat(Y, "-01-01").

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH RECURSIVE Years AS (
    SELECT 2018 AS report_year
    UNION ALL
    SELECT report_year + 1 FROM Years WHERE report_year < 2020
)
SELECT p.product_id,
       p.product_name,
       CAST(y.report_year AS CHAR) AS report_year,
       (DATEDIFF(
           LEAST(s.period_end, DATE(CONCAT(y.report_year, '-12-31'))),
           GREATEST(s.period_start, DATE(CONCAT(y.report_year, '-01-01')))
       ) + 1) * s.average_daily_revenue AS total_amount
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN Years y ON s.period_start <= DATE(CONCAT(y.report_year, '-12-31'))
            AND s.period_end >= DATE(CONCAT(y.report_year, '-01-01'))
ORDER BY p.product_id, report_year;
```

complexity.notes: Joining sales intervals with a fixed 3-year recursive sequence executes in linear time proportional to S.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Attempting to expand day-by-day generates millions of intermediate rows.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Interval clipping with LEAST and GREATEST computes overlap days in a single mathematical expression.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Date boundary clipping using LEAST and GREATEST functions joined against distinct years.

hints.title: Player Score Accumulation across Matches
hints.text: A player earns points whether participating as the first player or second player in a match.

hints.title: Score Union Stack with Group Ranking
hints.text: Vertically stack first and second player match scores using union all. Rank players within each group ordered by points descending and player identifier ascending.

hints.title: Tournament Winner Blueprint
hints.text: with TotalScores as (select player_id, sum(score) as score from (select first_player as player_id, first_score as score from Matches union all select second_player as player_id, second_score as score from Matches) s group by player_id), Ranked as (select p.group_id, p.player_id, row_number() over (partition by p.group_id order by coalesce(t.score, 0) desc, p.player_id asc) as rn from Players p left join TotalScores t on p.player_id = t.player_id) select group_id, player_id from Ranked where rn = 1.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
WITH TotalScores AS (
    SELECT player_id, SUM(score) AS score
    FROM (
        SELECT first_player AS player_id, first_score AS score FROM Matches
        UNION ALL
        SELECT second_player AS player_id, second_score AS score FROM Matches
    ) s
    GROUP BY player_id
),
Ranked AS (
    SELECT p.group_id, p.player_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY p.group_id
               ORDER BY COALESCE(t.score, 0) DESC, p.player_id ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Players p
    LEFT JOIN TotalScores t ON p.player_id = t.player_id
)
SELECT group_id, player_id
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
```

complexity.notes: Stacking match scores and computing partitioned row ranking executes in linear-logarithmic time.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Evaluating only first player scores misses points earned by the same athlete when competing as guest.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Union all unrolls dual match roles into a unified scoring stream prior to window ranking.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Use of UNION ALL to combine host and guest roles, and ROW_NUMBER() with player_id tie breaker.

import pandas as pd

def tournament_winners(players: pd.DataFrame, matches: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    m1 = matches[['first_player', 'first_score']].rename(columns={'first_player': 'player_id', 'first_score': 'score'})
    m2 = matches[['second_player', 'second_score']].rename(columns={'second_player': 'player_id', 'second_score': 'score'})
    scores = pd.concat([m1, m2]).groupby('player_id')['score'].sum().reset_index()
    merged = players.merge(scores, on='player_id', how='left')
    merged['score'] = merged['score'].fillna(0)
    sorted_df = merged.sort_values(by=['group_id', 'score', 'player_id'], ascending=[True, False, True])
    res = sorted_df.drop_duplicates(subset=['group_id'], keep='first')
    return res[['group_id', 'player_id']]
solutions.approach: Pandas Concat Scores and Group Partition Sort

hints.title: Hierarchical Node Role Classification
hints.text: Nodes in a tree hierarchy are distinguished by their structural positioning: root has no parent, inner has both parent and children, and leaf has a parent but no children.

hints.title: Conditional Branching on Parent Roles
hints.text: Inspect p_id for null to detect root. Then test whether the node identifier appears as a parent elsewhere in the tree using in with a non-null subquery.

hints.title: Case Expression Blueprint
hints.text: Select id, case when p_id is null then 'Root' when id in (select p_id from Tree where p_id is not null) then 'Inner' else 'Leaf' end as type from Tree.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT id,
       CASE
           WHEN p_id IS NULL THEN 'Root'
           WHEN id IN (SELECT p_id FROM Tree WHERE p_id IS NOT NULL)
               THEN 'Inner'
           ELSE 'Leaf'
       END AS type
FROM Tree;
```

variables: N: number of nodes in Tree
complexity.notes: Case expression evaluating parent presence and subquery membership.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Omitting WHERE p_id IS NOT NULL in the subquery causes IN (NULL, ...) to evaluate to UNKNOWN, misclassifying leaves.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Deduplicating parent IDs in memory evaluates node roles in linear time.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Filtering nulls from the subquery to ensure NOT IN / IN evaluates deterministically.

import pandas as pd

def user_purchase_platform(spending: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    grouped = spending.groupby(['spend_date', 'user_id']).agg(
        platforms=('platform', set),
        amount=('amount', 'sum')
    ).reset_index()
    def get_plat(p_set):
        return 'both' if len(p_set) == 2 else list(p_set)[0]
    grouped['platform'] = grouped['platforms'].apply(get_plat)
    agg_user = grouped.groupby(['spend_date', 'platform']).agg(
        total_amount=('amount', 'sum'),
        total_users=('user_id', 'count')
    ).reset_index()

    dates = spending['spend_date'].unique()
    grid = []
    for d in dates:
        for p in ['desktop', 'mobile', 'both']:
            grid.append({'spend_date': d, 'platform': p})
    grid_df = pd.DataFrame(grid)
    res = grid_df.merge(agg_user, on=['spend_date', 'platform'], how='left')
    res['total_amount'] = res['total_amount'].fillna(0).astype(int)
    res['total_users'] = res['total_users'].fillna(0).astype(int)
    return res

complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Inner join only categorizes countries with recorded November observations.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Date range filtering and conditional CASE statement on aggregate AVG.

solutions.code:
SELECT c.country_name,
       CASE 
           WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) <= 15 THEN 'Cold'
           WHEN AVG(w.weather_state) >= 25 THEN 'Hot'
           ELSE 'Warm'
       END AS weather_type
FROM Countries c
JOIN Weather w ON c.country_id = w.country_id
WHERE w.day BETWEEN '2019-11-01' AND '2019-11-30'
GROUP BY c.country_id, c.country_name;
solutions.approach: Date Range Join with Conditional Case Aggregation

```mysql
SELECT c.name
FROM Candidate c
JOIN Vote v ON c.id = v.candidateId
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY COUNT(v.id) DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

import pandas as pd

def winning_candidate(candidate: pd.DataFrame, vote: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    top_candidate = vote['candidateId'].value_counts().index[0]
    winner = candidate[candidate['id'] == top_candidate]
    return winner[['name']]
